Photograph: Kacey Chapman/Reuters US midterm elections 2026 Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears Project will prepare volunteers across US to monitor polls, encourage early voting and respond to disinformation Rachel Leingang Mon 14 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 14 Sep 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies. The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation. The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races. Trump promise of $5,000 for US citizens after midterms decried as ‘bribery’ Read more These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Each state party has a trained election protection director. The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant. The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC, said the project is much more extensive and coordinated than the party has been in the past on election protection. “We didn’t want to be caught flat-footed on election day or leading up to election day,” she said. These volunteers will be trained to “be happy” and respond to any voter needs, including helping them find a polling location if they’re in the wrong place, or informing them they can cast provisional ballots if they need to, Kleeb said. They will also document whether others at the polls are hindering voters. “We don’t know if there are going to be a bunch of insurrectionist types out there trying to intimidate voters, but we’re going to be there happy with information, but we’re also going to be there trained to document if the other side is doing things that are violating the law,” she said. The party will additionally push out its first national early-vote campaign, telling voters to “bank their vote” by casting ballots early by mail or in person. This will include ad campaigns focused on communities at risk of Republican election interference. The state parties and the DNC typically run get-out-the-vote programs, but this year’s will include more explicit directions to voters – telling them to vote early, and not let a mail ballot sit on their kitchen counter for weeks before turning it in, Kleeb said. The party will also push for people to vote early in person. “We don’t know what Donald Trump is going to do. We’ve heard some of the things that he may do, but none of us can predict his behavior,” she said. “He’s so chaotic. All of us have witnessed certainly that. So the earlier you can vote, the better.” The third part of the project will spin up a “democracy defense network”, led by Democratic strategist Simon Rosenberg, designed to identify and counter tactics that can sway elections, including disinformation, dark money, manipulation via artificial intelligence and election subversion. The network will allow state parties to communicate with each other about these threats to share knowledge, with a goal to get ahead of such tactics before they gain traction. https://volumeone.org/articles/2026/09/1.text: Home Events Calendar Submit an Event Articles & Photos Past Issues Features Food & Drink Restaurants Bars Contests & Deals Contests Daily Restaurant Deals Best Of Best of the Chippewa Valley Advertise Regional Editions Check Out Chippewa Falls Check Out Menomonie Local Guides/Lists Health, Fitness, & Wellness Outdoors & Recreation Student City Guide Weddings & Occasions Best of Summer View All (30+) » Volume One Events Summer Concert Series Restaurant Week Chalkfest Winter After Hours Best Night, Party True North, Storytelling Hullabaloo, Kids Concerts More by Volume One The Local Store Shop Online Gallery / Rental Chippewa Valley Family Magazine / Website Kids/Family Events Volume One Tickets Browse Upcoming Events Sell Tickets for your Event Community Initiatives Vanguard Awards Think Eau Claire Culture & Entertainment in the Chippewa Valley Q&A: Happy Sweet 16 To Lazy Monk Brewing! now in its teenage years, the Eau Claire brewery owners share words of wisdom and funny anecdotes from its longtime patrons Thursday Sep. 17th, 2026 Evelyn Nelson , photos by Andrea Paulseth Lazy Monk Brewing has officially hit the 16-year mark! This age, for many, is a major milestone – and while we definitely don't advocate driving under the influence, Lazy Monk will officially be driving into its next chapter. Based in Eau Claire, the brewery continues to serve dozens of signature European-style brews to its Chippewa Valley patrons. Sept. 12 gave Eau Claire locals much to celebrate. Thousands gathered for the 37th annual downtown Fall Festival while, just a few minutes away, an area park hosted a frisbee gold fundraiser . Others spent the afternoon at Lazy Monk Brewing ’s “Sweet 16” anniversary party, cooling down with a taste of the brewery’s newly released premium lager. Looking back 16 years to the business’s beginnings, owners Theresa and Leos Frank recalled just starting out – brewing, taste testing, packaging and delivering their beer. What started out as a few cans has grown into a staple refreshment of many local businesses and beer lovers. Their operations first began in a homemade brewhouse, which has since evolved into a welcoming destination along Madison Street where friends and families gather, Theresa shared. We sat down with Theresa for a quick Q&A on all things Lazy Monk: what beers remain coveted by longtime fans, what inspired the husband and wife to dive head first into brewing, their time spent abroad and much more as we celebrate its 16-year anniversary. “We want to be a small brewery supplying the best product we can – we never lost track of that. That’s still where we are (today) and we’re very happy. We feel like we’ve made it.” –Theresa Frank, co-owner of Lazy Monk Brewing V1: Looking back to year one , when Lazy Monk first began, was there a specific moment that solidified your calling to brew locally? TF: “My husband (Leos) worked for a company in Chippewa Falls, he had been there for years and never saw layoffs coming and even he was laid off. … We went for a walk and sat on this bench by Banbury (Place) and I said, ‘well, what do you want to (be) when you grow up?’ and he said, ‘you know, I really want to brew.’ That was really the moment and once Leos is passionate about something, he takes it full throttle.” “And so, we did. It was a leap of faith I’ll tell you that. (Leos) worked it all: he brewed, he delivered, he packaged, he did everything. The man was burning at both ends, but the reality is it we saw something and it continued to grow.” “We want to be a small brewery supplying the best product we can – we never lost track of that. That’s still where we are (today) and we’re very happy. We have 10-12 employees and we can support them. We feel like we’ve made it.” Each September, Lazy Monk Brewing's tap room has been redecorated with an Oktoberfest theme for its annual celebration. Plus, we can't forget the German-style pretzels, bratwursts, spätzle, traditional regalia and live music (Lazy Monk's 2013 Oktoberfest celebration, pictured). V1: You’ve mentioned international travels and European communities that are centered around beer drinking. In what ways do those inspirations manifest into the experience at Lazy Monk? TF: “There are so many because (Leos) drags me from brewery to bar when we’re in Europe. It’s (about) taking those times when we’re there to talk to the brewers, the breweries and see what’s being done there – both traditionally, as well as anything new. (We’re) able to bring that back here and duplicate it in our brewery to give people that taste who may not have the opportunity themselves to travel to Europe – to taste that fresh beer.” “One of the biggest (differences) is the natural fermentation and natural carbonation. A lot of people force carbonation. The last time we were in Europe was last April, we (visited) quite a few breweries and we came back with a beer called the ‘Fresh 12.’ The Fresh 12 is very similar to our pilsner, except the process (does) not force carbonation. We allow it to happen naturally and it’s now a regular staple on our menu because people appreciate the fact that we aren't rushing just to make the almighty dollar. We're taking time to do the process correctly and to do it the ‘old world way’ and it really reflects in that beer.” We're taking time to do the process correctly and to do it the 'old word way' and it really reflects in that beer. V1: Speaking of the taps, are there any coveted Lazy Monk brews that longtime fans constantly request, or perhaps a unique creation that Leos has stored away for good? TF: “There is a beer called ‘Theresa’s Sunshine’ that I have lots of requests (for) to come back, but my husband doesn’t want to do it anymore… I’m not sure why! We have a smoked tobacco (brew) that people love and we bring that back every couple of years. We do listen to (customers) and we bring things back. Some of them aren’t the best sellers but we know we have a group of people that want it, so we’ll go ahead and put it on the rotation.” “For our anniversary, we’re coming out with our ‘Sweet 16’ anniversary beer, which is something that my husband – who is the brewer – is very excited about, to showcase what we’ve learned through the years. It’s a premium lager, it is a light golden in color … about 30 IBUs. (It’s) something you would find as a premium lager overseas in the Czech Republic.” If you're a Lazy Monk regular, you know these signature mugs all too well. Its longtime "Mug Club" welcomes patrons to exclusive access and full pours in a designated mug during visits to the taproom. Plus, $1 off a 4-pack purchase of beer, among other perks. Learn more about the program and how to sign up, online . V1: For those who might not know, the brewery’s walls are chock full of faces and memories from customers and family, past and present. Walking past them today, is there a particular snapshot that immediately brings a smile to your face? TF: “There’s one that always sticks out to me and people ask (about) because our son now also works sometimes at the brewery. There’s a picture of him in our very first brewhouse … we have (a) picture of him peeking up over the top of the boil kettle. He’s standing in it, barely comes to the top of it and (then) there’s my husband. Now I see him (and) he towers over my husband. So every time I walk by that photo, I always have to smile and say, ‘yep, we’ve been here 16 years.’ ” V1: The taproom can often feel like a second home for your “regulars.” What are some reasons that contribute to this environment today? TF: “Quite frankly there's so, so many different groups that come in that are all special and very unique. We’re about to have our fifth wedding for people who met at the brewery or have met through friends through the brewery – and they want to get married there. That right there solidifies we’re building relationships and it’s not just us. It’s the people who come in and they sit by each other because we want to encourage that. The next thing we know, damn if we’re not having another wedding.” “The other big thing that’s really special to Leos and I is when you’re in Europe, people stop by the pub to have a beer and they have their groceries and their kids… but people stop in because bars are not taboo. We are a family place and nothing makes you feel better. On Sundays, there’s a gentleman who has been coming in since before he was married – as a matter of fact they were married in our (brewery). They now have a child … they bring their children in, the children play games, they drink their beer – that’s just what we are. That’s the type of environment that we have, where people feel comfortable, and we’re very proud.” We're about to have our fifth wedding for people who met at the brewery or have met through friends through brewery – and they want to get married there. That right there solidifies we're building relationships and it's not just us. V1: What might be the things you and Leos look forward to as Lazy Monk begins its next 16 years of business in the Chippewa Valley? TF: “To get through Oktoberfest , that’s my wish now. Every day we’ll just continue to do the best job we can for our friends and family at Lazy Monk. We really don’t know when it’s going to end, but until then, we’re going to be working every day, making sure that everyone’s happy and we take care of everyone.” Lazy Monk Brewing's outdoor patio (pictured) features European-style, hand-illustrated decorations to its exterior. Patrons can also find real hop plants growing all along the perimeter, adding a fresh and herbal aroma to the drinking experience. This Q&A has been lightly edited for publication. Lazy Monk Brewing (97 W Madison St.) is a family friendly bier hall and bier garden that overlooks the Chippewa River in downtown Eau Claire. Open seven days a week, Monday from 4-9pm; Tuesday-Friday from 4-10pm; Saturday from noon-10pm; Sunday from noon-9pm. Follow along with the brewery's Facebook page to view new event updates and beer releases. This website is brought to you by Volume One Magazine - Culture and Entertainment in the Chippewa Valley . https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c9dr8k.text: 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight 'Very upsetting': Residents in shock after historic French town hall set alight Close A historic town hall in the French city of Limoges has been damaged in an apparent arson attack following a day of nationwide protests on Saturday. Dramatic footage shared online shows the 19th-century building engulfed in flames, with the spire of its clock tower later collapsing. On Sunday, stunned residents watched as firefighters, who had battled the blaze through the night, assessed the building's structural integrity. Officials have not yet confirmed whether the town hall is at risk of collapse. "Damaging heritage buildings because you're angry with the government is selfish", one resident told the BBC. BBC correspondent Chris Bockman reports from Limoges. Read more about the protests across France. https://www.dw.com/en/espionage-accusati.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PR1c Prefer DW on Google Yonca Verdioglu Sik (right) after her release with her husband, journalist and MP Ahmet Sik (left) Image: ANKA Advertisement When police officers appeared at her home in Istanbul last Wednesday evening, Yonca Verdioglu Sik was surprised — even more so when they took her in for questioning. Her lawyer says she was accused of political and military espionage. But, according to transcripts of the interrogation that were published later, Verdioglu Sik was never asked any questions about espionage. Instead the public prosecutor's office appeared to be more interested in the activities of the German organization, the Heinrich Böll Foundation, for whom Verdioglu Sik works. For 18 years, Verdioglu Sik, who was born and raised in Germany, has been the foundation's project coordinator. In her role, she organizes projects that focus on democracy and women's, minority and LGBTQ+ rights. During the interrogation, transfers of money from the foundation into her bank account were discussed. Verdioglu Sik found out that she was now subject to a travel ban too. Pressure on politicians Verdioglu Sik was eventually released. Nonetheless her arrest caused outrage among critics of the Turkish government. Sik is married to investigative journalist and member of parliament, Ahmet Sik. He belongs to the left-wing Workers' Party of Turkey, or TIP, and is known as one of the current government's harshest critics. Recently Sik has been looking into a stock market scandal , which allegedly benefitted members of the ruling Justice and Development Party, or AKP , headed by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and their associates. Opposition critics drew a clear conclusion: As a member of parliament, Sik has parliamentary immunity. So instead, the justice system is putting pressure on him through his wife. "If you take away a state's law, what is left is no longer called a state, but a gang," Sik responded to the arrest in writing. Verdioglu Sik's arrest is not the first such case in Turkey . Ever since the attempted coup against the Erdogan government in 2016, accusations of espionage have been levelled at a wide variety of groups in Turkey: journalists, opposition figures and human rights activists as well as employees of foreign embassies and staff of foreign institutions like non-governmental organizations and foundations. Diplomatic disputes Such accusations were often followed by acquittals or convictions for other offenses, albeit sometimes years later. What the many instances have in common though is what's known as a "chilling effect." Any investigation can mean lengthy pre-trial detention, reputational and professional damage and even social isolation. In the past such cases have even triggered diplomatic spats . For example in 2015, Can Dundar and Erdem Gul, both senior journalists at the opposition daily Cumhuriyet , were accused of espionage after reporting that Turkey had tried to ship arms to rebels fighting the Syrian government. Dundar now lives in exile in Berlin. In 2017, Erdogan said that reporter Deniz Yücel , then working for German newspaper Die Welt , was a "German agent." That led to a serious diplomatic crisis between Berlin and Ankara. Journalist Deniz Yücel was labeled a "German agent" by Turkey's president Image: Bernd Elmenthaler/IMAGO IMAGES Espionage charges have also been laid against local employees of the US diplomatic corps and against a lawyer working for the German embassy. US pastor Andrew Brunson and his wife were also arrested because of alleged links to Kurdish anti-government groups . Turkish philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala, who was charged with espionage and attempting to overthrow the constitutional order, remains in prison. Most recently, espionage charges have been brought against the former Istanbul mayor and Erdogan's political competitor, Ekrem Imamoglu, and a number of journalists. 'Hostage diplomacy' Hakki Tas, a research fellow and expert on Turkey at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies, or GIGA, notes that the number of such cases have been increasing over the past few years. On the one hand, Turkey has the right to protect itself from foreign intelligence services — especially given geopolitical competition and conflict in the region, he argues. On the other hand, there's a long tradition of bringing the Turkish opposition to court to face security charges. "What foreigners or employees of foreign institutions have experienced in recent years is a continuation of this pattern," Tas told DW. LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Media outlets and NGOs critical of the government have faced investigations, trials and other sorts of state sanctions for years. The ruling AKP party has also brought in its own version of a so-called "foreign agent law." These sorts of espionage cases serve both a domestic and foreign policy function, Tas observes. For locals, "contact with a foreign institution, foreign funding or even a perfectly normal salary could become part of an investigation someday," Tas explains. "For opposition figures and civil society organizations, in particular, this can become a security issue." In terms of foreign policy, the cases also show other countries that there are limits to their activities inside Turkey. These kinds of accusations seem to become more frequent when there's some sort of foreign policy tension — for example, after Western criticism of how opposition groups were dealt with after the alleged coup in 2016, the aforementioned disputes about arms deliveries in connection with Syria , or criticism from abroad about the removal of elected mayors in Turkey. It can also serve as a kind of "hostage diplomacy," Tas says. US pastor Andrew Brunson (center, white shirt) with his wife after his release in 2018 Image: Getty Images/AFP/B. Kilic Punishing process The case of US cleric Brunson is a good example. After his arrest, the Turkish government proposed a trade with the Americans. They wanted to exchange Turkish preacher Fethullah Gulen, who lived in the US and who the Turkish government blamed for the 2016 coup attempt. This suspicion of foreign institutions isn't something that the Erdogan government invented, Tas points out. In the early 2000s, several representatives of German organizations were already standing trial in Turkey. At the time, it was alleged that, among other things, the German spy service was using German foundations as a front for conspiracy. In some of the best-known cases, defendants often don't end up convicted of espionage. The Kavala case demonstrates this. He was initially acquitted of espionage several times and spent two years in prison, just because of those charges. But Tas says that's no surprise, referring to a 1979 work about the sociology of law written by US law professor Malcolm Feeley. It's title: "The Process Is the Punishment." This story was originally published in German. No future in Turkey? https://hvg.hu/vilag/20261114_jovo-heten.text: Jövő hét csütörtökön találkozik egymással Donald Trump amerikai, Vlagyimir Putyin orosz és Hszi Csin-ping kínai elnök - jelentette be a Fehér Ház helyi idő szerint pénteken. A tájékoztatás szerint a háromoldalú találkozóra a dél-kínai Sencsen városában rendezendő Ázsiai és Csendes-óceáni Gazdasági Együttműködés (APEC) csúcs margóján kerül sor. Trump a többi között a nukleáris leszerelés, valamint az iráni konfliktus kérdését is felveti majd Putyinnak, azonban várhatóan nem kerül sor az ukrajnai háborúval kapcsolatos megbeszélésekre – közölte a Fehér Ház egyik tisztségviselője a sajtóval. A tisztségviselő ezt azzal indokolta, hogy Trump és Putyin nem fognak kétszemközt találkozni. Peking korábban fenntartásait fejezte ki a háromoldalú nukleáris leszerelési tárgyalásokkal kapcsolatban. A kínai vezetés azzal érvelt, hogy az ország nukleáris képességei nem mérhetők össze az Egyesült Államokéval és Oroszországéval, ezért jelenleg nem tartaná méltányosnak, észszerűnek és reálisnak az ilyen tárgyalásokhoz való csatlakozást. Kormányzati források szerint a találkozón Trump várhatóan nem említi fel Jensen Huang, az amerikai Nvidia chipgyártó vállalat volt vezérigazgatójának ügyét, aki azt követően kényszerült lemondani , hogy egy feltételezett kínai kémmel folytatott házasságon kívüli kapcsolata nemzetbiztonsági aggályokat vetett fel . Amerikai tisztségviselők azt mondták, az elnököt Elon Musk amerikai techmilliárdos is elkíséri Kínába. Hétfőn kezdődő, négynapos ázsiai körútja során során Trump a Fülöp-szigeteket is útba ejti, ahol találkozik az Egyesült Államokat, Indiát, Japánt és Ausztráliát tömörítő Quad csoport vezetőivel. 5 071 632 000 forint, 2 658 350 euró, 1 257 100 dollár.
